outputs.challenge: the starting question or topic (always available)
outputs.stakeholders: a map of who is involved
outputs.deep_story: the deep story / myth under the problem
outputs.values: a map of value and money flows
outputs.team: a team that works well together
outputs.story: a story or pitch that moves people
outputs.backlog: user stories for a build team

T: The team disagrees on what the problem is
The brief already contains a solution
st: Gather what you know about users and context.
Test it with the team; adjust the scope.
TB-07.w: A solution disguised as a problem.
TB-07.wh: One sentence naming who has the problem, what it is and why it matters.
TB-07.u: Starting a project, or the team disagrees on what to solve.

T: Ideas are starting to compete with no yardstick
Kick-off: agree what good looks like
st: Collect values and insights that matter.
Check each one guides a real decision.
Post them where the team works.
TB-08.w: Generic principles that rule nothing out.
TB-08.wh: A short list of guidelines the team agrees to design by.
TB-08.g: A yardstick for every later decision.

T: There is no shared way to judge ideas or tests
People mean different things by "success"
st: Ask what success means for users, business, team.
Turn each into a measurable sign.
Set the level that counts as success.
TB-27.wh: Agreeing up front how success will be seen and measured.
TB-27.u: Before ideation, so ideas can be judged fairly.
TB-27.g: Shared criteria to judge ideas and tests.

T: Starting a workshop or project with a new group
People need a frame they all sign up to
st: State the challenge and why it matters.
PB-04.w: A brief that already holds the solution.
PB-04.wh: A short frame for the challenge: goal, scope, users and constraints.
PB-04.g: A frame everyone signs up to.

T: Unsure which method or metric fits this stage
Someone wants to measure scale before the problem is proven
st: Map each risk to its layer.
Pick the method that reduces it.
MX-01.w: Measuring scale before the problem is proven.
MX-01.wh: Four risk layers — design thinking, lean start-up, ecosystem, scale — each method reducing a different risk.
MX-01.u: Choosing which method and metrics fit your stage.
MX-01.g: The right method and metric per risk.

T: You need a baseline to show progress
Someone asks "how will we know it worked?"
st: Ask what success means for user, business, team.
MX-02.wh: A template to set measurable success criteria at the start of the cycle.
MX-02.g: A baseline to measure progress against.

T: The problem needs to be testable and trackable
Funders want evidence behind the problem
MX-03.wh: A structured problem statement whose relevance you can measure.
MX-03.g: A problem you can test and track.

T: A quick check of social and planetary alignment
Comparing ideas or strategies by impact
st: Go through the questions as a team.
Mark where it is strong or weak.
HU-01.w: Treating it as a pass/fail form.
HU-01.wh: Questions that act as a strategic compass: check a project against people, planet and future generations.
HU-01.u: Diagnosing any project, idea or strategy quickly.

T: The problem is huge, messy and contested
Many groups disagree on what is wrong
st: Break it into parts and causes.
HU-25.w: Pretending it can be solved once.
HU-25.wh: Deconstructing a complex problem with no single right answer to find a starting point.
HU-25.u: The problem is huge, messy and contested.

T: Starting an initiative that should scale
People need a purpose that pulls them in
HU-44.wh: A short, bold, memorable purpose statement that rallies people.
HU-44.u: Starting an initiative that aims to scale.
HU-44.g: A purpose that pulls people in.

T: Many groups are involved and you do not know who matters
Someone quiet or powerless may be missing
st: Place them in rings: core, direct, indirect.
Decide who to involve or interview.
TB-15.w: Missing the quiet or powerless groups.
TB-15.wh: A visual map of every person and organisation with a claim on the problem.
TB-15.u: The project touches many groups and you need to know who matters.
TB-15.g: A shared picture of who is in the system.

T: The problem depends on more than one user
You need the big picture around the problem
st: Put the user or topic in the middle.
TB-26.w: Mapping everything — focus on what matters.
TB-26.wh: A map of the user’s wider context — people, places, tools, rules and trends.
TB-26.u: The problem depends on more than one user.
TB-26.g: The big picture around the problem.

T: Futures or systems work where many actors shape the outcome
Nature or future generations need a seat
st: Note objectives and what’s at stake.
HU-04.wh: A visual map of all actors linked to a challenge and the relationships between them.
HU-04.g: A living map of who shapes the future.

T: You need a full scan of outside forces
Policy, technology or economic shifts may change the problem
st: Feed the key ones into scenarios.
HU-05.w: A long list with no priorities.
HU-05.wh: Scanning Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environmental forces.
HU-05.u: You need a complete scan of the macro environment.
HU-05.g: A full picture of external forces.

T: Surface fixes keep failing
A belief, myth or stigma drives the problem
st: Rebuild worldview and systems from it.
HU-08.wh: Digging from the visible litany through systems and worldview to myth — then rebuilding.
HU-08.g: Deep drivers and a new narrative.

T: Judging whether a solution is safe and just
Social and ecological limits matter
HU-30.wh: Kate Raworth’s model: stay above the social foundation and below the ecological ceiling.
HU-30.u: Judging if a solution is safe and just.
HU-30.g: A safe, just space to design in.

T: You need to know where impact is biggest
Materials, waste or supply chains are involved
st: List inputs and outputs per stage.
HU-32.w: Ignoring use and end of life.
HU-32.wh: A qualitative map of a product’s environmental impact across its life stages.

T: First step of any systems analysis
The scope keeps creeping or is unclear
st: Frame the problem and its history.
Decide what is in and what is out.
Map the key actors and elements.
HU-36.wh: Defining what is in and out of the system — and mapping its actors.
HU-36.u: The first step of any systems analysis.

T: You need to see what keeps the system stuck
Fixes keep backfiring
st: List variables that can go up or down.
Find loops; label R or B.
HU-37.w: Variables that can’t rise or fall.
HU-37.wh: Linking variables into reinforcing (R) and balancing (B) loops.
HU-37.u: You need to see what drives a system’s behaviour.
HU-37.g: A map of the system’s feedback.

T: Choosing where to intervene
Only shallow fixes are on the table
st: Start from your causal loop diagram.
Rank them from shallow to deep.
Pick a mix you can act on.
HU-38.wh: Finding where a small push changes the whole system — from numbers to mindsets.

T: Money or value flows decide what happens
Designing or understanding an ecosystem
st: Tag each flow: money, social, ecological.
HU-39.wh: A map of how value — financial, social, ecological — flows between actors.

T: Before scaling up
Worried about side effects
st: Amplify the good, limit the harm.
HU-47.wh: Foreseeing the indirect, often unintended effects of scaling a technology.

T: You need the problem from the user's side
You only have assumptions about people
st: Prepare a question map, from easy to deep.
Ask open questions; ask for stories.
Debrief with the team right after.
TB-09.w: Leading questions and pitching your idea.
TB-09.wh: An open conversation to understand a person’s experiences, feelings and motives.
TB-09.u: You need to see the problem from the user’s side.

T: The problem space is still fuzzy
You are not sure what to ask yet
st: Pick a topic, not a question list.
Meet people in their own context.
Follow their story; ask “tell me more”.
TB-10.wh: A loosely guided interview to explore a user’s world before you know what to ask.
TB-10.u: Early, while the problem space is still fuzzy.

T: An answer feels shallow
A problem keeps coming back
st: Start with an observed behaviour or problem.
Ask why and write the answer.
Ask why of that answer; repeat.
Stop at a real motive or root cause.
TB-11.wh: Asking “why?” up to five times to move from a symptom to a root motive.
TB-11.u: An answer feels shallow or a problem keeps coming back.
TB-11.g: A root cause or deeper need.

T: Scoping a problem or planning research
There are big gaps in what you know
st: Write the six questions around the topic.
Answer each with what you know.
TB-12.wh: Who, what, where, when, why and how — a checklist to see a situation whole.
TB-12.u: Scoping a problem or preparing an interview.
TB-12.g: A full picture and a list of open questions.

T: Design for the progress people seek, not features
People use workarounds you do not understand
st: Pick a situation where the user struggles.
Write: “When…, I want to…, so I can…”.
Add the emotional and social sides.
Find where today’s solutions fail the job.
TB-13.w: Describing your product instead of the job.
TB-13.wh: A lens on the “job” a customer hires a product to do — functional, social, emotional.
TB-13.u: You want to design for the progress people seek, not features.
TB-13.g: Clear jobs to design and measure against.

T: Average users tell you nothing new
Some groups are where the system breaks first
st: Define the extremes on key dimensions.
Translate edge needs into mainstream insight.
TB-14.wh: Learning from people at the edges — heavy users, non-users, people ahead of the market.
TB-14.u: Average users can’t tell you anything new.
TB-14.g: Needs the average user can’t yet name.

T: People struggle to put feelings into words
Shame or fear is part of the problem
st: Prepare cards with emotions or images.
Ask the user to pick cards for a moment.
Ask why they chose each card.
TB-16.w: Reading the card instead of asking why.
TB-16.wh: Cards with feelings or images that users pick to show how something makes them feel.
TB-16.u: Users struggle to put emotions into words.

T: You have done interviews and need to make sense of them
The team needs a shared view of a user
st: Put the user in the middle.
Fill says, does, thinks, feels from research.
TB-17.wh: A canvas for what a user says, does, thinks and feels — plus pains and gains.
TB-17.u: After interviews, to make sense of what you heard.
TB-17.g: A shared, human view of the user.

T: The team needs one person to design for
People keep designing for themselves
st: Give one a name, face, context and quote.
Check against real data; update often.
TB-18.w: Stereotypes with no research behind them.
TB-18.wh: A fictional but research-based profile of a typical user, with needs and goals.
TB-18.u: The team needs one person to design for.
TB-18.g: A user the whole team keeps in mind.

T: You need to find where the experience breaks
A process over time has drop-off points
st: Pick a persona and a scenario.
Add actions, thoughts and an emotion curve.
TB-19.w: Mapping the ideal, not the real journey.
TB-19.wh: A step-by-step map of what a customer does, thinks and feels across touchpoints.
TB-19.u: You need to find where the experience breaks.

T: Going into the field and need to know what to look for
People say one thing and do another
st: Prepare a sheet with the five headings.
Observe and note under each heading.
Photograph or sketch what you see.
TB-20.wh: An observation frame: Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects, Users.
TB-20.u: You go into the field and need to know what to look for.
TB-20.g: Structured field notes, ready to cluster.

T: You have big data and want design insight
Numbers and stories do not connect
st: Match each to the data you have.
Bring the results back to the team.
TB-21.wh: A guide for turning design questions into questions data analysis can answer.
TB-21.u: You have big data and want design insight from it.
TB-21.g: Data findings linked to user insight.

T: Outsiders would change how people behave
A community distrusts researchers
st: Give them simple tools and prompts.
Let them observe in daily life.
TB-22.wh: Users observe and interview their own peers, who open up more at eye level.
TB-22.u: Outsiders would change how people behave.

T: Moving from research to ideas
The team needs an open, inspiring question
st: Check: not too broad, not too narrow.
Pick the best one to brainstorm.
TB-24.w: Hiding a solution inside the question.
TB-24.wh: Reframing an insight as an open “How might we…?” question to ideate on.
TB-24.g: A question that sparks many ideas.

T: Others need to understand and feel the findings
You need buy-in from decision makers
st: Pick the audience and one message.
TB-25.w: Stories with no real data behind them.
TB-25.wh: Telling insights and ideas as stories with a hero, a conflict and a resolution.
TB-25.u: Others need to understand and feel your findings.
TB-25.g: Insights people remember and act on.

T: Before prototyping, to know what to test
Too many features and no focus
st: Plan prototypes and tests around them.
TB-29.w: Listing everything — then nothing is critical.
TB-29.wh: A shortlist of the few things a solution must get right, from the user’s view.
TB-29.u: Before prototyping, to know what to test.

T: The team needs a shared picture of the user
A persona workshop with a group
st: Base it on interviews and observation.
Give a name, face, context and quote.
PB-05.wh: A realistic profile of one user — needs, goals, context — to design for.
PB-05.u: The team needs a shared picture of the user.
PB-05.g: A user the team designs for.

T: Designing something people should come back to
A habit or loop drives the behaviour
st: Name the internal and external triggers.
Ask what users invest that brings them back.
PB-06.wh: A canvas for habit-forming products: trigger, action, variable reward, investment.
PB-06.u: Designing something people should come back to.
PB-06.g: A map of the habit loop.

T: Why do people choose one option over another?
Design around motives, not features
st: Write: when…, I want to…, so I can….
PB-07.wh: Framing what the customer is trying to get done — the progress they seek.
PB-07.u: You want to know why people choose a product.
PB-07.g: Jobs to design and measure against.

T: Making sense of interviews and observation
Facilitating synthesis with a group
st: Put the user in the middle.
PB-09.wh: A canvas for what the user sees, hears, thinks, feels, says and does.
PB-09.u: Making sense of interviews and observation.
PB-09.g: A shared, human view of the user.

T: Observing in the field
Raw notes need structure
st: Prepare a sheet with five headings.
Ask how and why it happens.
PB-10.wh: Observing Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects, Users — asking what, how, why.

T: You need real needs, not wishes
Interviews keep producing feature requests
st: Turn what you hear into need statements.
PB-12.wh: Open conversations that uncover needs people may not say directly.
PB-12.u: You need real needs, not wishes.
PB-12.g: Real needs in the user’s words.

T: You want tomorrow's needs today
Some people already hack the system
st: Find people who feel the need early.
See what they built or hacked.
PB-13.w: Mistaking a niche for the market.
PB-13.wh: Learning from users ahead of the market who often build their own fixes.

T: Scoping or planning research
The team jumps straight to solutions
PB-14.wh: Who, why, what, when, where, how — six questions to see a problem in full.
PB-14.u: Scoping a problem or planning research.
PB-14.g: A full picture and a research plan.

T: Designing digital experiences you cannot observe
Relying only on analytics
st: Map their feelings at each step.
Use data to find where emotions dip.
PB-17.wh: Bringing empathy methods into digital product and UX design.
PB-17.u: Designing digital experiences where you can’t see the user.

T: Synthesising before choosing a point of view
Research feels one-sided
st: Note each one’s view of the problem.
PB-18.w: Only taking the team’s own view.
PB-18.wh: Looking at the problem from every angle: users, stakeholders, context, tech, business.
PB-18.u: Synthesising before you define a point of view.
PB-18.g: A rounded understanding of the problem.

T: Structuring insights across time and scale
Seeing the past, present and future of a use case
st: Put the topic in the centre window.
Fill past/future and the levels around it.
PB-19.wh: A 3×3 grid of past–present–future × sub-system–system–super-system, plus a daisy map to cluster needs.

T: Moving from research into ideation
Facilitating a point of view with a group
PB-20.w: A solution hidden in the question.
PB-20.wh: A sentence of user + need + insight, turned into “How might we…?”.

T: Handing needs to an agile build team
Requirements are vague
PB-21.w: Stories with no real user behind them.
PB-21.wh: An agile format: As a [role], I would like [action], so that [benefit].
PB-21.u: Handing needs to agile development teams.
PB-21.g: Needs developers can build and test.

T: You need stories that move people
Pitching an idea emotionally
st: Imagine a suitcase and an object inside.
Ask who packed it, and why.
Link it to your user or idea.
PB-39.w: A story unrelated to the user.
PB-39.wh: Imagining objects in an old suitcase to invent emotional stories.
PB-39.u: You need stories that make people feel something.

T: Synthesis needs traceable evidence
Reporting what you learned
st: Fill sees, hears, thinks, feels, says, does.
Note how many sources back each point.
MX-05.wh: A template to capture and synthesise what you learn about the user.

T: Show how much the team learned from users
Leaders doubt the research was done
st: Track numbers per week and phase.
Ask: are we talking to users enough?
MX-06.wh: Counting and tracking the team’s interactions with customers and users.
MX-06.u: You want to show how much the team learned from users.

T: Define what to measure from the customer's view
Success metrics are company-centric
st: Write each job as a statement.
MX-07.w: Jobs written from the company’s view.
MX-07.wh: The jobs customers try to get done — the basis of the metrics they judge success by.
MX-07.u: Defining what to measure from the customer’s view.

T: Looking for big opportunities
Rank jobs by importance and satisfaction
MX-08.wh: Finding jobs that matter a lot but are badly served — where breakthroughs hide.

T: Personas that grow with evidence
Personas never get updated
st: Write assumed traits, jobs, pains, gains.
Mark each as assumed or validated.
MX-09.wh: A persona template for stating — and then testing — assumptions about users.
MX-09.g: Personas that gain evidence over time.

T: Choosing which users to focus on, with data
Segments compete for attention
st: Score and chart them side by side.
MX-10.w: Criteria that don’t matter to the decision.
MX-10.wh: Comparing personas or segments with numbers on chosen criteria.
MX-10.u: Choosing which users to focus on.
MX-10.g: A data-backed choice of target users.

T: Designing physical, digital or hybrid experiences
You need a measurable focus list
MX-11.wh: The few items an experience must get right.
MX-11.u: Designing physical, digital or hybrid experiences.

T: Prototyping over several cycles
Track progress per critical item
st: Set a measure per critical item.
MX-12.wh: Tracking how well each critical item performs across iterations.
MX-12.g: A progress chart per critical item.

T: Moving from research to ideation with evidence
The question must be evidence-based
MX-13.wh: Reframing the challenge into an actionable problem statement.

T: Lots of data, no clear insight
The team analyses forever
st: Analyse: sort and break down the data.
MX-14.wh: The move from breaking data apart (analysis) to building insight (synthesis).
MX-14.u: Lots of data, no clear insight.

T: Check the team's bias before futures or systems work
The team all looks and thinks alike
st: Learn common biases as a team.
Spot them in your own assumptions.
HU-06.w: Believing bias can be removed fully.
HU-06.wh: Becoming aware of the mental shortcuts that distort how we see the future.

T: Decisions rest on hidden assumptions
People jump from data to conclusions
st: Start from the action or belief.
Climb down: what data did we select?
Name the meanings and assumptions added.
HU-07.wh: A model of how we climb from data to assumptions, beliefs and actions.

T: Too many signals and trends to handle
You need a prioritised short list
HU-10.wh: Sorting possible events by how likely and how impactful they are.
HU-10.u: Too many signals and trends to handle.

T: Signals pile up after scanning
Looking for where change is going
st: Group those pointing the same way.
HU-11.wh: Clustering many signals into meaningful patterns.
HU-11.u: After scanning, when signals pile up.
HU-11.g: Patterns that show where change is going.

T: The team must interpret what it found together
Findings conflict
st: Frame a narrative for each pattern.
Ask how it emerged and where it leads.
Agree what it means for you.
HU-12.wh: Creating shared meaning from patterns — turning foresight into insight.
HU-12.u: The team must interpret what it found.

T: Designing for people who do not exist yet
Long horizon, changing users
st: Profile who lives there: role, values, quote.
Add needs, pains and hopes there.
HU-22.w: Today’s person in a sci-fi costume.
HU-22.wh: A detailed persona living inside a future scenario.
HU-22.u: Designing for people who don’t exist yet.

T: Complex problems with many actors
Empathy for staff and institutions, not only users
st: Map what each thinks, feels, says, does.
HU-23.wh: An empathy map for a whole system, not one user.

T: Synthesising empathy across a system
Each actor's view sits in its own silo
st: List who is impacted, nature included.
Fill how the system thinks, feels, acts.
Name the norms and beliefs behind it.
HU-24.wh: A canvas that gathers many actors’ views — including environments and future generations.
HU-24.g: A collective picture of the system.

T: Designing value beyond the customer
Value for people and planet
st: Profile user, society, planet: pains, gains.
Check for harm to any of them.
HU-26.wh: A value proposition for the user, society and the planet.

T: A solution could reach millions
Effects differ at each scale
st: Note challenges and benefits at each.
HU-48.wh: Empathy at scale — person, community, society — for a widely adopted technology.

T: The solution must work in the future, not just today
Trends may change the problem
st: Collect social, tech, market and policy trends.
Ask what each means for your users.
TB-23.wh: Spotting and judging the trends that will shape users and markets.
TB-23.u: The solution must work in the future, not just today.
TB-23.g: A view of the forces ahead.

T: You need a long-term vision, not a fix
History explains where this is heading
st: Look back: how did the topic evolve?
Draw the cone forward from today.
Place trends and futures inside it.
Pick a desirable future to aim for.
TB-28.w: Assuming the future is a straight line.
TB-28.wh: A cone that looks back at the past to project possible futures.
TB-28.u: You need a long-term vision, not just a fix.
TB-28.g: A future vision rooted in history.

T: You have a good HMW and need ideas
The team needs lots of options fast
st: Rules: defer judgment, go for quantity.
One idea per note; build on others.
TB-30.wh: A group session to generate many ideas fast, without judging.
TB-30.u: You have a good HMW question and need ideas.

T: Too many ideas and you need to prioritise
Compare effort against impact
st: Choose two criteria, e.g. impact and effort.
Place each idea together as a team.
TB-31.w: Axes that don’t help the decision.
TB-31.wh: Two axes, four boxes — to sort ideas or spot strategic patterns.
TB-31.u: Too many ideas and you need to prioritise.

T: The team must choose quickly and fairly
Stalemate on which idea
st: Lay out the ideas where all can see.
Vote silently and at the same time.
Discuss the top ideas, then decide.
TB-32.wh: Everyone gets a few dots to vote for the ideas they favour.
TB-32.u: The team must choose quickly and fairly.

T: Loud voices dominate brainstorms
Quiet people have ideas too
st: Seat six people, each with a 3-column sheet.
Write three ideas in five minutes.
Pass the sheet; build on the ideas.
Repeat six rounds — up to 108 ideas.
TB-33.wh: Six people write three ideas in five minutes, then pass the sheet on and build.

T: Brainstorms keep giving the same ideas
You need wild options
st: Flip or adapt the strange ideas.
Add the best to your idea pool.
TB-34.w: Not bringing wild ideas back to the problem.
TB-34.wh: Brainstorm variations — reversal, worst idea, random words — that break habits of thought.
TB-34.u: Normal brainstorming keeps giving the same ideas.

T: Stuck inside your own field's thinking
Someone else already solved a similar problem
st: Abstract the problem to its core challenge.
Find fields that face the same challenge.
TB-35.w: Copying the surface, not the principle.
TB-35.wh: Borrowing solutions from other industries or worlds that solved a similar problem.
TB-35.u: You are stuck inside your own industry’s thinking.

T: Explain an idea quickly and convincingly
Compare ideas side by side
st: Approach: how does the idea solve it?
Benefit: what value for the cost?
TB-36.wh: A one-page pitch structure: Need, Approach, Benefit, Competition.
TB-36.u: You must explain an idea quickly and convincingly.
TB-36.g: A crisp idea summary you can compare.

TB-37.n: Blue ocean tool & buyer utility map
T: The market is crowded and ideas look alike
You need differentiated value
st: List what the industry competes on.
Map buyer utility across the experience.
Shape an offer with a new value curve.
TB-37.w: Differentiating on what buyers don’t value.
TB-37.wh: Tools for finding uncontested market space by changing what competitors take for granted.
TB-37.u: Your market is crowded and ideas look alike.

T: One make-or-break assumption could sink the idea
Test the riskiest part first
st: Build the fastest thing that tests it.
Keep, change or drop the idea.
TB-38.w: Polishing it — rough is the point.
TB-38.wh: A rough prototype that tests only the one function the idea depends on.
TB-38.u: One make-or-break assumption could sink the idea.

T: Ideas feel safe and too similar
Push a bolder direction
st: Pick an idea that seems too crazy.
Ask what would need to be true.
Test it and harvest the surprises.
TB-39.wh: A prototype of the wild, risky option the team would normally discard.
TB-39.u: Ideas feel safe and too similar.
TB-39.g: A breakthrough insight or bolder direction.

T: Several partial findings need combining
Merge directions into one
TB-40.w: Mixing so much that nothing is clear.
TB-40.wh: A prototype that mixes the learnings of earlier experiments.
TB-40.u: You have several partial findings to bring together.

T: Align on direction before building
Stakeholders need to see the vision
st: Show the vision as story, video or mock-up.
Test it with users and stakeholders.
TB-41.w: Treating the vision as the final spec.
TB-41.wh: The big picture of the future solution, made tangible.
TB-41.u: Moving from exploring to building, to align on direction.

T: The vision is set, now prove the core works
Ready for functional detail
st: Pick the functions that matter most.
Build them so they really work.
Fix and expand step by step.
TB-42.wh: A first working version of the key functions.
TB-42.u: The vision is set and you need to prove it works.

T: One part needs detail to be judged
A detailed test of a critical part
st: Choose the X that needs detail.
Test X in the context of the whole.
TB-43.w: Choosing the easiest X, not the riskiest.
TB-43.wh: One part — X — is built in full detail while the rest stays rough.
TB-43.u: Part of the solution needs detail to be judged.
TB-43.g: A detailed test of one critical part.

T: Before handover or launch
The solution is ready to implement

TB-04.wh: A sheet of 30 empty circles to turn into objects in three minutes.
TB-04.u: You want to show that quantity beats perfection.
TB-04.g: Proof that fast, many ideas is a skill.

T: Energy is low and the room needs movement
Afternoon slump
st: Stand in a circle in a ninja pose.
Take turns: one move to tag a hand.
The target gets one move to dodge.
Tagged hands go behind the back; last ninja wins.
TB-05.w: People who can’t move — offer them a role.
TB-05.wh: A fast standing game of strike and dodge, without contact.
TB-05.u: Energy is low and the room needs movement.
TB-05.g: Energy, laughs and a playful mood.

T: Show why early prototyping beats planning
The team over-plans
st: Hand out spaghetti, tape, string, one marshmallow.
Debrief: who tested early, who planned?
TB-06.w: Skipping the debrief — that’s the point.
TB-06.wh: Teams build the tallest tower of spaghetti and tape with a marshmallow on top.
TB-06.u: You want to show why early prototyping beats planning.
TB-06.g: A felt lesson in iterating early.

T: Before any workshop
Plan a session that runs well
st: Define the goal and the outcome.
TB-67.w: Too many methods for the time.
TB-67.wh: A canvas to plan a workshop: goal, people, agenda, methods, materials, room.
TB-67.g: A workshop that runs to plan.

T: Planning a design sprint
The team needs a rhythm
st: Observe users; define a point of view.
PB-01.w: Running it once and calling it done.
PB-01.wh: The six-step loop — Understand, Observe, Point of view, Ideate, Prototype, Test — run as one unit.
PB-01.g: A repeatable rhythm for the team.

T: Bringing the mindset into a busy organisation
A light process for non-designers
PB-03.wh: Swisscom’s three-step micro cycle: hear the customer, create solutions, deliver and validate.
PB-03.u: Bringing the mindset quickly into a busy organisation.
PB-03.g: A light process anyone can adopt.

T: Before interviews or tense discussions
Listen with less bias
st: Stay with what the person says.
Reflect afterwards on what you missed.
PB-15.wh: Paying attention on purpose — to the user and to your own judgements.

T: People talk over each other
Some voices never get heard
st: Speaker holds the stick and speaks.
Next speaker restates what they heard.
PB-16.wh: Only the person holding the stick speaks; others listen until they can restate it.

T: Explain or capture ideas visually
Words are not landing
st: Learn a few simple icons and figures.
PB-38.wh: Sketching ideas to make them visible and discussable — “think with the pen”.

T: A heated or stuck discussion
Conflict blocks progress
st: Let people speak in any order.
Capture on four charts as they talk.
Follow the energy, not the agenda.
PB-43.wh: Facilitation that follows the group’s energy, capturing problems, solutions, concerns and data as they come.

TB-54.n: I like, I wish, I wonder
T: Quick reflection after a session, prototype or pitch
You need balanced feedback in minutes
st: Capture and agree on next steps.
TB-54.wh: Three simple prompts for open, kind and constructive feedback.
TB-54.u: Reflecting on a session, prototype or pitch.

T: End of a sprint or phase
What helps and what hinders us?
st: Draw island, boat, wind, anchors, rocks.
Team adds notes to each part.
Pick actions for the next cycle.
TB-55.wh: A boat drawing: wind pushes you on, anchors hold you back, rocks are risks, the island is the goal.
TB-55.u: End of a sprint or project phase.
TB-55.g: A shared view of what helps and hinders.

T: End of a project or phase
Knowledge must outlive the project
st: Ask what went well and what didn’t.
Write lessons the next team can use.
TB-58.wh: A structured look back at what worked, what didn’t, and why.
TB-58.u: End of a project or major phase.

T: Planning a whole project, not just a sprint
Leave room to explore
st: Build and test a vision prototype.
PB-02.wh: The big journey: many micro cycles that diverge, pass the “groan zone”, then converge on a vision.
PB-02.u: Planning a whole project, not just a sprint.
PB-02.g: A plan that leaves room to explore.

T: End of each cycle or sprint
Improve the way you work
PB-37.wh: Four fields: continue, stop, try out — and what doesn’t matter.
PB-37.u: End of each cycle or sprint.
PB-37.g: Clear actions to improve the process.

T: Many people need to share and grow ideas
A community or stakeholder gathering
st: Set tables, each with a question.
Rotate; a host stays to summarise.
PB-41.wh: Small groups discuss a question at tables, then rotate and build on each other’s talk.
PB-41.u: Many people need to share and grow ideas.
PB-41.g: Collective insight from a big group.

T: A large group and a complex topic
People need ownership
PB-42.wh: Participants set the agenda and join the sessions they care about.
PB-42.u: Large groups, complex topics, high energy.

T: A team starts working with shared goals
Goals and roles are unclear
st: List team objectives and key results.
MX-55.wh: A canvas to align a team’s mission, roles and OKRs.
MX-55.u: A team starts working with OKRs.
MX-55.g: A team aligned on goals and roles.

T: Turn objectives into key results
You need a team pact
st: Write each KR: from X to Y by when.
Check it is an outcome, not a task.
Agree the team’s ways of working.
MX-59.wh: Writing measurable key results and agreeing how the team works.
MX-59.g: Clear key results and a team pact.

T: Right after goals are set
Skills gaps block the goals
MX-61.wh: Reflecting on the skills and capabilities the team needs.
MX-61.g: A skills plan linked to goals.

T: Launching goals to a wider group
People do not know the goals
MX-62.wh: A canvas for how OKRs are communicated and owned.
MX-62.u: Launching OKRs to a wider group.

T: Measurement feels forced or ignored
The culture resists the goals
st: Ask how people experience the metrics.
Adjust the system or the habits.
MX-64.wh: Reflecting on how the measurement system fits the culture.

T: You are new to this field or organisation
The brief is vague and you do not know what to ask
st: Start from a wide question or topic.
Scan talks, reports, social media and a few internal interviews.
Turn what you found into sharper research questions.
SD-01.w: Hunting for answers instead of questions.
SD-01.wh: Your own digging before fieldwork: the sector, the organisation, similar services and how the sponsor sees the problem.
SD-01.u: Before you plan any research, to find the right questions.
SD-01.g: Better questions and a first picture of the field.

T: Someone has probably studied this already
You need numbers and sources behind the problem
st: List promising sources: papers, reports, datasets, experts.
Search for qualitative and quantitative data.
Summarise what is already known, with sources.
Mark the gaps your own research must fill.
SD-02.wh: Collecting and summarising research that already exists on the topic.
SD-02.u: At the start of every research loop, before primary research.
SD-02.g: What is already known, and the gaps.

T: Channels, places or systems matter as much as people
The service spans several organisations and platforms
st: Choose the perspective and scope of the map.
List actors: people, organisations, places, channels, machines.
Arrange them by sector and closeness.
Draw relationships or value exchanges; mark gaps to research.
SD-03.w: One giant map for every purpose. Make several focused ones.
SD-03.wh: A map of every actor around a service, people and non-people (places, channels, devices, platforms), and how they relate or exchange value.
SD-03.u: A stakeholder map leaves out the things and channels that shape the service.
SD-03.g: One picture of the whole service ecosystem.

T: Insiders know the system better than you do
Whose view of the system counts is itself the question
st: Invite people who know one clear perspective; bring your research.
In small groups: list, prioritise and place stakeholders.
Present, compare and merge; note what to verify.
SD-04.w: Who you leave out decides whose view is missing.
SD-04.wh: A workshop where people who know the system build the stakeholder or system map themselves.
SD-04.u: The team cannot see the whole system from its own desk.
SD-04.g: A system map the participants own.

T: You have never used the service you are redesigning
You need a quick first read before recruiting anyone
st: Decide which experience, where and when.
Go through it for real, across the channels involved.
Note what you see and hear on one side, what you feel and interpret on the other.
SD-05.w: Treating your own experience as everyone's.
SD-05.wh: You go through the experience yourself, as a customer or an employee, and document it.
SD-05.u: Early, before interviews, so you can interpret what people later tell you.
SD-05.g: First-hand field notes and a feel for the experience.

T: People speak more freely online than to a researcher
A community already discusses this problem in public
st: Pick the communities that fit your question.
Decide how to record: screenshots, notes, maps.
Observe; add online interviews if useful.
Compare what people say online with what they do offline.
SD-06.w: Quoting people without thinking about consent and privacy.
SD-06.wh: Studying how people talk and act in online communities around the topic.
SD-06.u: The people you need gather online, or the experience itself is online.
SD-06.g: Quotes and patterns from real online behaviour.

T: What people say and what they do differ
Staff workarounds hold the service together
st: Choose who, where, when and how you will document.
Plan how you will start, end and limit your effect on them.
Watch, and ask people to explain actions and objects in the moment.
Note what they do not do, and gaps between words and actions.
SD-07.w: Forgetting that being watched changes behaviour.
SD-07.wh: Spending time inside people's work or life: shadowing, a day in the life, working alongside.
SD-07.u: You need to see what people do, not only hear what they say.
SD-07.g: Rich notes on real behaviour in context.

T: People cannot describe the process from memory
The setting itself is part of the problem
st: Decide who, when and where; plan how to record the setting.
Ask people to demonstrate the concrete experience.
Follow up on gestures, objects and surroundings.
SD-08.w: Holding it in a meeting room and losing the context.
SD-08.wh: An interview held where the experience happens, so people can show as well as tell.
SD-08.u: You need needs, hidden networks or a specific experience explained in place.
SD-08.g: Stories and evidence tied to a real setting.

T: You need to see queues, waits and drop-offs as they happen
Asking questions would change what people do
st: Plan who observes, where, when and for how long.
Stay in the background; do not interact.
Record actions, and what people avoid or ignore.
Count simple things, such as people per hour or people who give up.
SD-09.w: Covert observation where consent is needed.
SD-09.wh: Watching behaviour as a fly on the wall, without interacting.
SD-09.u: To balance interview bias and count what really happens.

T: The journey runs over days or weeks
You need many people's experiences, not five interviews
st: Plan incentives; recruiting is the hard part.
Give short, clear instructions and profile questions.
Let participants report as things happen.
Review entries as they arrive and start clustering.
SD-10.w: Instructions so long that nobody keeps reporting.
SD-10.wh: Many participants document their own experience on their phones, step by step, with text, photos and ratings.
SD-10.u: The experience runs over days or across places you cannot follow.
SD-10.g: Time-stamped, located entries from many people.

T: The topic is private, at home or hard to talk about
You need to cross a cultural gap you do not understand
st: Design the kit: instructions, notebook, camera, prompts.
Send it; let people document for days or weeks.
Review it together with each participant in an interview.
SD-11.w: Reading the material without asking the person what it means.
SD-11.wh: A package of small tasks (diary, camera, prompts) that people complete on their own, with no researcher present.
SD-11.u: A researcher in the room would distort things, or life at home is out of reach.
SD-11.g: Self-documented material from inside people's lives.

T: Staff and users each know a different part of the journey
You need a shared starting map to plan research
st: Set the main actor and scope; invite people who know the journey.
In small groups: stages, then steps.
Add an emotional line or other lanes.
Merge the maps; mark every step as assumed or researched.
SD-12.w: Treating a workshop map as proven. It is assumption-based.
SD-12.wh: A workshop where customers and frontline staff map the journey themselves.
SD-12.u: You need a first journey map and the people who live it are available.
SD-12.g: A draft journey map owned by the people in it.

T: Data is scattered across people and files
The team needs to see all the evidence at once
st: Print the data and put it up.
Cluster by topic, segment, journey step or problem.
Name the clusters; look for links between them.
Turn patterns into personas, maps and insights.
SD-13.w: Clustering only what confirms your first idea.
SD-13.wh: All research data on one wall (quotes, photos, screenshots, statistics, artifacts), clustered until patterns show.
SD-13.u: After fieldwork, when data sits in separate notebooks and files.
SD-13.g: Visible patterns and a shared place for the research.

T: Findings are long and nobody can repeat them
Ideation needs a sharp tension to work on
st: Write first insights: [actor] wants to [action] because [motivation], but [tension].
Link each insight to the raw data behind it.
Collect more data wherever an insight is thin.
SD-14.w: A neat sentence with no data behind it.
SD-14.wh: Each main finding written as one sentence: who wants to do what, why, and what gets in the way.
SD-14.u: You have patterns and need findings others can act on.
SD-14.g: A short list of evidence-backed insights.

T: The research will be challenged by decision makers
Every finding so far comes from one kind of source
st: List each finding and where it came from.
Tick: methods used, data types, who collected it.
Flag findings that rest on a single source.
Plan one extra method or researcher for the flagged ones.
SD-15.w: Calling three interviews by one person "research".
SD-15.wh: A check that each finding rests on more than one method, more than one type of data and more than one researcher.
SD-15.u: Before you build on findings from a small or one-sided study.
SD-15.g: A list of which findings are solid and which are single-source.

T: People who were not in the field must act on the findings
A funder or agency needs the research on record
st: Decide who reads it and what it is for.
State who was involved, the methods and the number of loops.
Summarise key findings with raw data as evidence.
Have other researchers or participants review it.
SD-16.w: Conclusions with the raw evidence stripped out.
SD-16.wh: The process, methods, data and insights pulled into a report shaped for its readers.
SD-16.u: Research must travel beyond the people who did it.
SD-16.g: Findings other teams can trust and reuse.

T: The challenge is too big to brainstorm on
Ideas stay vague because the question is vague
st: Pick a way to slice: viewpoints, attributes, the W questions, repeated whys.
Invite people who know the background or will deliver.
Ideate on each; then check what the parts add up to.
SD-17.w: Slicing so finely that the system view is lost.
SD-17.wh: Breaking one oversized ideation challenge into smaller ones, for example by viewpoint, attribute or question.
SD-17.u: The ideation theme is too big or abstract to get a grip on.
SD-17.g: Several manageable challenges with different angles.

T: The journey map shows where things break
Ideas need to connect to real steps, not float
st: Put up the current-state map and its research.
Spot the critical steps, using research, personas or a quick walkthrough.
Ideate around each critical step; note ideas and questions.
Draw rough new maps; check how each change affects the rest of the journey.
SD-18.w: Polishing single steps and missing the whole arc.
SD-18.wh: Using a current-state journey map as the trigger for ideas, one critical step at a time.
SD-18.u: You have a journey map and want ideas grounded in it.
SD-18.g: Ideas tied to specific steps of the journey.

T: The problem lives between actors
One missing or weak relationship blocks everything
st: Take one system map at a time.
Ask: which relationship could be stronger? Which exchange could we enable?
Ask what happens if an actor is removed, added or changed.
Draw a future-state map for the best ideas.
SD-19.w: Ideas that make the map prettier but help no actor.
SD-19.wh: Using a stakeholder, value network or ecosystem map as the trigger for ideas.
SD-19.u: The opportunity sits in relationships, not in one touchpoint.
SD-19.g: Ideas that change relationships and flows.

T: Ideas stay abstract and need to become visible
You need breadth and depth in one short session
st: In table teams, silently sketch about ten rough concepts.
Share briefly; the team picks one interesting sketch.
Sketch ten variations of that one.
SD-20.w: Drawing metaphors instead of real-world solutions.
SD-20.wh: A fast sketching round for breadth, then a second round that goes deep on one sketch.
SD-20.u: Ideating on concrete situations or interfaces.
SD-20.g: Around twenty concrete sketches: one broad set, one deep.

T: The problem is physical or interpersonal
The session needs empathy and energy
st: Immerse the group in the context first.
Act out one at a time; try alternatives as they come up.
Record ideas and bugs after each run.
SD-21.w: Sliding back into discussion instead of acting.
SD-21.wh: Acting out a situation with your body to find problems and ideas.
SD-21.u: The challenge is physical or between people.
SD-21.g: Ideas and a bug list from lived situations.

T: Hundreds of notes and little time
People cling to their own ideas
st: Stand people in rows facing the wall.
The front row sorts, the second row advises.
Break up oversized clusters; rescue orphan notes.
SD-22.w: A few people doing all the sorting.
SD-22.wh: A group sorts a wall of sticky notes in rotating rows, so everyone handles the material.
SD-22.u: Many notes and a large group.
SD-22.g: Sorted clusters and a group that knows the content.

T: A large group needs to choose in minutes
Authors defend their own ideas
st: Each person holds one idea sheet.
Mingle and swap sheets until the music stops.
In pairs, split 7 points between your two sheets.
Repeat five times; add up the scores.
SD-23.w: Sheets that are unclear to a stranger.
SD-23.wh: People swap idea sheets while moving, then pairs split seven points between two sheets; five rounds rank everything.
SD-23.u: A big group must rank many options fast.
SD-23.g: A ranked list and shared ownership of the ideas.

T: Ideas need owners, not only votes
Forming working groups for the next step
st: Lay ideas on the floor or keep them on the wall.
People stand on, or touch, their favourite.
Look at the groups: too big, too small, unbalanced?
Ask which important idea nobody chose.
SD-24.w: Popular ideas crowding out important ones.
SD-24.wh: People show support by standing on, or pointing at, the idea they back; groups form around ideas.
SD-24.u: Choosing ideas and forming working groups at once.
SD-24.g: Selected ideas with a team behind each.

T: Separate ideas need to become one experience
People need to see before and after
st: Redraw the steps as they should happen.
Mark what must change to move from current to future.
SD-25.w: An ideal journey that ignores backstage reality.
SD-25.wh: A journey map of the experience as it should be, set against the current-state map.
SD-25.u: Ideas need to be joined into one coherent experience.
SD-25.g: A concept shown as an end-to-end experience.

T: The service is a human encounter, not a screen
A fragile moment must go right the first time
st: Pick a key scene; set a rough stage and props.
Play it; replay and comment until it is understood.
Change one thing; replay and compare.
Keep a list of bugs, insights and ideas.
SD-26.w: Changing the scene before understanding it.
SD-26.wh: A key scene of the service is played out and replayed, changing one thing at a time.
SD-26.u: The service depends on behaviour, tone and space.
SD-26.g: A tested service scene and a bug list.

T: People say "it's fine" and mean something else
Shame, fear or status shape the encounter
st: Run a key scene and freeze at one statement.
Ask: what is the unspoken thought behind it?
Ask for the thought behind that thought; repeat.
At each level, ask how the service could respond.
SD-27.w: Inventing subtext with no research behind it.
SD-27.wh: In a rehearsed scene, stopping at one line and saying aloud what the person really means, level by level.
SD-27.u: Polite words hide the real need.
SD-27.g: Chains of unspoken needs and new openings for value.

T: The service spans many places and people
You want to test the whole flow in an hour
st: Draw a map of the locations; choose a figurine per actor.
Pick a story and play it through, speaking the dialogue.
After each run, note what to change.
SD-28.w: Moving figures without acting out the interactions.
SD-28.wh: The whole service played on a tabletop map with figurines, like a small theatre.
SD-28.u: You need to test an end-to-end service cheaply.
SD-28.g: A tested end-to-end flow with variants.

T: A kiosk, counter, room or device is part of the service
People need to walk through the space
st: Build the object or space from simple materials.
Split into users, operators and observers.
The user acts; operators simulate the object's response.
List bugs and ideas; rebuild and repeat.
SD-29.w: Spending time on looks instead of use.
SD-29.wh: Objects or spaces mocked up in cardboard, with people playing the machine's reactions.
SD-29.u: A physical object or space is part of the service.

T: The team jumps to screens too early
The digital service should feel like a good conversation
st: One person plays the app as a knowledgeable helper.
Afterwards, decide how to turn it into screens.
SD-30.w: Acting like a machine instead of a helpful person.
SD-30.wh: A person plays the app or website as a conversation, before any screens exist.
SD-30.u: Before wireframes, to find what the digital service should say and do.
SD-30.g: The right conversation before the interface.

T: You need to test a screen flow today
Design polish would be wasted at this stage
st: Sketch every key screen and pop-up.
A user "clicks" with a finger; an operator swaps the paper.
Photograph the sketches and link them in a prototyping app.
SD-31.w: Explaining the screen to the user.
SD-31.wh: Hand-drawn screens tested by hand, then photographed and linked into a clickable model.
SD-31.u: A quick test of an interface before design.

T: Nobody can say in one line why people would want it
The team disagrees on the core value
st: Brainstorm the facts and the emotional hook.
Sketch a few adverts on large paper.
Show them to outsiders; collect reactions.
SD-32.w: A clever slogan that hides what the service does.
SD-32.wh: A mock advert for the new service, shown to people who have not heard of it.
SD-32.u: You need to test whether the value is clear and wanted.
SD-32.g: A sharper value proposition and outsider reactions.

T: The new service changes who exchanges what with whom
People need to rearrange the system with their hands
st: Cut out and label the key elements.
Place them to model the system.
Draw relationships and exchanges between them.
Move, add and remove pieces to test variants.
SD-33.w: Keeping the model and forgetting what the team learned building it.
SD-33.wh: Paper cut-outs for people, places, channels and touchpoints, moved around a table to model the service system.
SD-33.u: You need to prototype how the whole system fits together.
SD-33.g: A shared, tested model of the service system.

T: Automation or AI is the idea, and building it is expensive
You must test value before investing in technology
st: Rig the set-up so responses look real.
SD-34.w: Wizards who respond better than the real system could.
SD-34.wh: Hidden operators fake the working parts so users believe the prototype is real.
SD-34.u: The core function is costly to build but cheap to fake.
SD-34.g: Evidence on core function and value before building.

T: Feedback turns into argument
Many groups must give feedback in little time
st: Clarifying questions only; keep it short.
Green: what to keep or grow.
Red: a concern is allowed only with a concrete suggestion.
The receiving team takes notes and says only "thank you".
SD-35.w: Criticism dressed up as a question.
SD-35.wh: A closed feedback round: clarifying questions, then what to keep (green), then concerns with a suggestion attached (red).
SD-35.u: Right after a presentation or prototype demo.
SD-35.g: Dense, usable feedback with no debate.

T: People shoot ideas down
Right before a brainstorm
st: Pair up and pick something to plan.
Round one: answer each offer with "yes, but…".
Compare how each round felt and what it produced.
SD-36.w: Skipping the comparison at the end.
SD-36.wh: Pairs plan something together, first answering every offer with "yes, but", then with "yes, and".
SD-36.u: Before ideation or any co-creative session.
SD-36.g: A felt difference between blocking and building.

T: Success depends on people doing something differently
Only usage is being measured
st: Write the success story you want to tell later.
Name the long-term outcomes, as specifically as you can.
List the behaviours that lead there and how you will know people used the solution.
Fix the data for each; measure a baseline.
BC-01.wh: The success story written first, then mapped backward: long-term outcomes, the behaviours that produce them, signs of use, and the data for each.
BC-01.u: At kick-off of anything meant to change behaviour.
BC-01.g: A chain from use, to behaviour, to outcome that you can measure.

T: People "know they should" but do not
Research keeps blaming willpower
st: Draft questions for capability, opportunity and motivation.
Add more questions where you expect the main blockers.
Make an observation checklist for the field.
BC-02.wh: Interview questions and an observation checklist built around capability, opportunity and motivation.
BC-02.u: Planning research on why a behaviour does not happen.
BC-02.g: A research guide that covers every type of blocker.

T: People start and then drop out
The system leaves people no real choice
st: Tag evidence of autonomy, competence and relatedness, met or frustrated.
Note which need the current system blocks most.
Write the needs to design for.
BC-03.wh: Reading the research for three basic needs: autonomy (real choice), competence (visible progress) and relatedness (feeling part of something).
BC-03.u: Making sense of why people engage or drop out.
BC-03.g: Need statements grounded in what motivates people.

T: You do not know why people do not do it
The team assumes people just need more information
st: Rows: blocker types under capability, opportunity, motivation.
Tag blockers that fit more than one row.
Rate how critical each one is.
BC-04.w: Forcing a blocker into one box.
BC-04.wh: A grid sorting everything that stops a behaviour into capability, opportunity and motivation, with the evidence beside each.
BC-04.u: After research, to diagnose why the behaviour fails.
BC-04.g: A diagnosed list of blockers with evidence.

T: Ten blockers and capacity for two
You need a defensible focus
st: Score each blocker 0 to 3 on each.
Choose the top few; name the ones you leave out.
BC-05.w: Choosing the easiest blocker, not the one that matters.
BC-05.wh: Scoring each blocker on a few criteria (how common, how often, how much it stops people, how solvable) to choose which to design for.
BC-05.u: There are more blockers than you can address.
BC-05.g: A short list of blockers to design against.

BC-06.n: Behaviour Change Wheel: pick the intervention
T: The team reaches for an awareness campaign by reflex
You need the type of solution before ideas
st: Take each prioritised blocker and its COM-B category.
Use the wheel's grid to shortlist intervention types.
Drop the types that are unethical or out of scope.
Note types that recur across blockers.
BC-06.w: Defaulting to education for every problem.
BC-06.wh: Matching each prioritised blocker to the types of intervention that work for it: education, training, persuasion, incentives, coercion, restriction, enablement, environmental restructuring, modelling.
BC-06.u: Moving from diagnosis to solution types.
BC-06.g: Solution types matched to the real blockers.

T: Ideas need to trace back to a diagnosed cause
Features are piling up without a reason
st: Add a column to the blocker grid for the chosen intervention type.
Ideate features that deliver that type.
Check each feature against the blocker it should remove.
Combine the features into one concept.
BC-07.w: Features with no blocker behind them.
BC-07.wh: Turning each chosen intervention type into concrete features, services or rules.
BC-07.u: You know the intervention type and need the actual design.
BC-07.g: A concept whose every feature answers a blocker.

T: People face the change alone
Family or peers undermine the change
st: Map who is helpful or unhelpful for the change.
List the kinds of help needed: practical, a partner, a listener.
Draft a specific request for each.
Add peers or experts where the existing network is thin.
BC-08.w: Using social features as a recruitment trick.
BC-08.wh: Helping people find who around them can help, and how to ask for something specific.
BC-08.u: Change is hard to do alone.
BC-08.g: Ideas that build support around the person.

T: Forms, plans or options overwhelm people
People drop out at a decision point
st: Find the decision points in the journey.
Make options comparable; show only the detail needed.
State the trade-offs; keep a way to choose later or opt out.
BC-09.w: Steering people toward what suits you.
BC-09.wh: Redesigning a decision so it is easier to make: fewer options, comparable options, just enough detail, clear structure and visible trade-offs.
BC-09.u: People stall, defer or choose badly at a decision point.
BC-09.g: A decision point people can get through.

T: Progress is invisible to the person making it
Feedback arrives too late to act on
st: Give feedback on the action, the pattern and the goal.
Set how often; always end with the next step.
BC-10.w: Rewards that invite gaming or punish steady performers.
BC-10.wh: Designing feedback in five steps: measure something, give feedback at several levels, show what others do, set a frequency, point to the next action.
BC-10.u: People cannot see their own progress.
BC-10.g: A feedback loop that supports growth.

T: People distrust the institution
The service needs sensitive information up front
st: Onboarding: say who you are and what the approach rests on.
Ask for data slowly and with permission; use plain language.
Design the exit as carefully as the entry.
BC-11.wh: Earning trust at the start, during use and at the end: explain the basis, protect data, ask permission, deliver value early, let people leave cleanly.
BC-11.u: People must share something sensitive or rely on you.
BC-11.g: A first-contact and exit design people can believe in.

T: The payoff is months or years away
People intend to act and never start
st: Link the goal to what matters to the person.
Break it into a near target.
Have them make and commit to a specific plan.
Mark small wins; change the environment to help.
BC-12.w: Goals set by the designer, not the person.
BC-12.wh: Making a distant goal feel close: tie it to what matters, bring the target nearer, commit to a concrete plan, start small, shape the environment.
BC-12.u: The benefit is far away and the effort is now.
BC-12.g: A goal-and-plan flow that keeps people going.

T: The design nudges, defaults or rewards
People in a weak position will use it
st: List every point where the design steers people.
Check: is the full picture told? Are the rules clear?
Check: can people decline, delay or leave?
Fix or remove anything that hooks rather than helps.
BC-13.w: Calling a dark pattern a nudge.
BC-13.wh: A check that the design leaves people in charge: the whole truth, clear rules, a way out, a "later" option, and choices tied to their own values.
BC-13.u: Before testing or launching anything that steers behaviour.
BC-13.g: An autonomy check and a list of fixes.

T: A funder asks whether it changed anything
Usage is high but outcomes are unknown
st: Take outcomes and behaviours from the logic map.
Pick the strongest design you can afford.
Plan the analysis before collecting data.
Compare with the baseline; report limits.
BC-14.w: Yes/no measures that hide partial progress.
BC-14.wh: Choosing how to show that the behaviour changed: a controlled trial, a real-world comparison, case studies or surveys, against a baseline.
BC-14.u: You must show it works, not only that it is used.

T: Everyone accepts "that's just how it's done"
A trend is changing the ground under the topic
st: List the key aspects of the topic.
Note the trends touching each aspect.
Write today's view for each: the convention (From).
Write the new view the trends point to (To), and the opening it creates.
KM-01.w: Writing a To that is only the From with nicer words.
KM-01.wh: A two-column table that sets today's accepted view beside a new view that current trends make possible.
KM-01.u: The problem is framed by habit and you need to question it before you scope.
KM-01.g: A reframed problem, with the conventions you are choosing to challenge.

T: The brief names a thing (a product, a form, a service)
You suspect the real issue is how people live, not the thing
st: Put the offering in the centre with its features.
Around it, list what people do with it and around it.
Around that, list the norms, rituals and meanings that shape those activities.
Look for openings in the two outer rings, not only the centre.
KM-02.w: Filling the culture ring with guesses about people you have not met.
KM-02.wh: Three rings around one offering: the thing, the activities around it, and the culture those activities sit in.
KM-02.u: A brief is stuck on the object and you need to widen the view.
KM-02.g: A wider frame: where the opportunity sits beyond the offering itself.

T: You have explored the topic and need a first point of view
The team cannot say in one breath what it is going after
st: Review the openings found so far.
Pick the ones worth pursuing and say why.
Take a position: who is it for, what need, what is new, what value.
Write it as a few plain sentences and share it for challenge.
KM-03.w: Treating the first statement as final. It is a hypothesis to revise.
KM-03.wh: A short written statement of what you intend to change, for whom, and why it matters now.
KM-03.u: After first exploration, before research is planned.
KM-03.g: A first innovation intent the whole team can point to.

T: "How did it get this way?" has no clear answer
Old rules still shape today's system
st: Choose the aspects to track (people, technology, rules, money…) and the time span.
Research what happened to each aspect over time.
Lay it out as a table: time across, aspects down.
Draw the lines where things shifted, name each era, and note what carries over.
KM-04.w: Naming eras before the research is in, then fitting facts to them.
KM-04.wh: A timeline table that divides the history of a topic into named eras and describes each one across the same aspects.
KM-04.u: You need history to understand why the system behaves as it does today.
KM-04.g: A map of eras and the shifts between them.

T: One organisation has to carry the change
You must judge whether the organisation can do this at all
st: State the intent you are judging the organisation against.
List strengths and weaknesses inside the organisation.
List opportunities and threats outside it.
Lay them on a 2×2 and discuss what it means for the intent.
KM-05.w: Four lists of opinions with no evidence. Mark each line: known or assumed.
KM-05.wh: A 2×2 of an organisation's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, read against one intent.
KM-05.u: Early, when the question is whether this organisation is placed to act.
KM-05.g: A sourced view of where the organisation stands.

T: Two or three fields are starting to overlap
New behaviour is appearing between sectors, owned by nobody
st: Choose the fields that touch your topic.
List the trends and new offerings in each field.
Draw the fields as overlapping circles and place each trend where it belongs.
Study the overlaps: what is emerging there, and who is absent?
KM-06.w: Drawing overlaps because the diagram looks good, not because anything is happening there.
KM-06.wh: Overlapping circles showing where separate fields are merging and what is emerging in the overlap.
KM-06.u: The opportunity or the problem lives between sectors.
KM-06.g: A picture of the overlaps and the openings inside them.

T: You need the whole system on one page
Things move between actors: money, information, goods, people
st: Entities: list the parts of the system (people, places, things).
Relations and flows: draw how the entities connect and what moves between them, with direction.
Attributes: add the key facts that describe each entity.
Refine with the team: what is missing, broken, one-way or overloaded?
KM-07.w: Drawing everything until nobody can read it. Set a boundary first.
KM-07.wh: A network diagram built from four parts: Entities, Relations between them, their Attributes, and the Flows that move through.
KM-07.u: After a stakeholder map, when you need to see how the system works, not only who is in it.
KM-07.g: A system diagram with its weak points marked.

T: You are about to pick who to interview
The easy-to-reach people are not the whole picture
st: List the kinds of people tied to the topic.
Choose two scales that describe how they differ (for example, how exposed and how much say).
Plot the kinds of people on the 2×2.
Check every corner is covered, then choose who to recruit and why.
KM-08.w: Recruiting only from the corner you already know.
KM-08.wh: A 2×2 of all the kinds of people around a topic, used to choose research participants on purpose.
KM-08.u: Before recruiting for interviews or observation.
KM-08.g: A recruiting plan that covers the range of people, with the gaps named.

T: You do not yet know where to aim the deep research
You need candidates for interviews
st: Write a short set of questions on activities, behaviour and attitudes.
Build the survey and send it to a broad group.
Look for patterns and surprises in the answers.
Choose focus areas and candidates for deeper study.
KM-09.w: Reading a quick, loose survey as proof. It only points to where to look.
KM-09.wh: A short, quick questionnaire used early to get an overview and to pick people and themes for deeper research.
KM-09.u: At the start of research, before interviews.
KM-09.g: Focus areas and a shortlist of people to study.

T: Field notes keep describing only what people did
You want one structured lens for observation
st: Prepare a note sheet with five headings: physical, cognitive, social, cultural, emotional.
Go into the field and observe or talk.
Write what you notice under each heading.
Read the five together and describe the person's overall experience.
KM-10.w: Filling the emotional and cultural boxes with your own assumptions.
KM-10.wh: An observation lens with five headings (physical, cognitive, social, cultural, emotional) that widens what you notice.
KM-10.g: Field notes that cover the whole person, not only the task.

T: The activity unfolds over time or in a noisy, changing place
The team needs to see it, not read about it
st: Decide what to film and who films: you or the participants.
Get informed permission from everyone who may appear.
Film the activity in its real setting.
Review the footage together and mark patterns.
KM-11.w: Filming people who have not agreed, or keeping footage longer than you said you would.
KM-11.wh: Filming people's activities in their real setting, then studying the footage for patterns.
KM-11.u: A process or a dynamic place needs to be studied more than once.
KM-11.g: Tagged footage and a list of observed patterns.

T: You cannot be there when it happens
You want people to lead the conversation, not you
st: Plan what people should photograph and for how long.
Brief them, hand over what they need, and check in midway.
Sit down together and let them talk you through each photo.
Debrief and note what surprised you.
KM-12.w: Interpreting the photos without the person who took them.
KM-12.wh: People photograph their own activities for some days, then explain the pictures to you in an interview.
KM-12.u: Life at home or on the move is out of reach for an observer.
KM-12.g: Photos with the participant's own account of each one.

T: Feelings and values are hard to say out loud
The topic carries shame, pride or stigma
st: Decide which attitudes you want to learn about.
Prepare a set of images open enough to carry many meanings.
Ask each person to sort them, in groups or along a scale, and to talk as they sort.
Record the sorts and the stories behind them.
KM-13.w: Choosing images that push people toward the answer you expect.
KM-13.wh: People sort prepared pictures and explain their choices, which brings out associations and values they would not state directly.
KM-13.u: You need attitudes and meanings, not behaviour.
KM-13.g: Sorted image sets with the reasons people gave.

T: The service or place does not exist yet
What people say they would do is not trustworthy enough
st: Choose one slice of the experience to simulate.
Build a rough stand-in: a room, props, people playing roles.
Run it with participants, watch what they do, and talk afterwards.
KM-14.w: Reading it as a test of the solution. It is research into what matters to people.
KM-14.wh: A staged version of an experience that lets you watch how people behave before anything real is built.
KM-14.u: You are studying a new service, place or interaction.
KM-14.g: Observed behaviour and what people said mattered to them.

T: A wall of notes and no meaning yet
Findings are descriptions, not explanations
st: Write each observation as a plain statement of what happened.
For each one, ask why, and agree on the most likely reason.
Write the insight as a general sentence that holds beyond this one case.
Group the insights and refine them together.
KM-15.w: Passing off an observation as an insight. If it does not say why, it is not one yet.
KM-15.wh: A step-by-step way to turn each field observation into an insight by asking why.
KM-15.g: A list of insights, each traceable to its observations.

T: Too many insights to hold in your head
Sticky-note clusters keep changing with whoever is in the room
st: List the insights along both sides of a grid.
Score how strongly each pair relates (0 to 3).
Reorder rows and columns so strong scores sit together.
Outline the clusters, name each one, and note how the clusters connect.
KM-16.w: Trusting the scores over judgment. The scoring is still opinion, only written down.
KM-16.wh: A scored grid that compares every insight with every other and shows which belong together.
KM-16.u: You have thirty or more insights and need a structure you can defend.
KM-16.g: Named clusters of insights and the links between them.

T: You need to compare many things at once: services, places, groups
"Where is the gap?" is the real question
st: Choose the two scales that matter most.
Plot each entity on the map.
Read it: clusters, empty areas, outliers, and who sits beside whom.
KM-17.w: Picking scales that make your favourite answer look good.
KM-17.wh: A two-scale map with many entities plotted on it, read for groupings and gaps.
KM-17.u: You have a set of comparable things and want to see the pattern.
KM-17.g: A position map with the gaps and clusters called out.

T: Many actors each do part of the work
Nobody can see how the pieces of work connect
st: List every activity seen in research, for all actors.
Score how closely each pair of activities relates.
Group the strongly related ones and name each group.
Draw the groups as a network and mark weak or missing links.
KM-18.w: Listing only users' activities and leaving out staff, partners and maintainers.
KM-18.wh: A network of everyone's activities, grouped by how closely they relate.
KM-18.u: Work is split across people or organisations and the joins are unclear.
KM-18.g: A network of activity clusters with the gaps marked.

T: People judge things by feel: safe or risky, warm or cold
You need to compare how different groups see the same thing
st: Choose what to compare: services, places, concepts or groups.
Define scales, each with two opposite words at its ends.
Mark every entity on every scale and join the marks into a profile line.
Compare the lines: where they split, where they match.
KM-19.w: Marking the scales yourself and calling it what users think.
KM-19.wh: A set of opposite-word scales on which several things are rated and compared as profile lines.
KM-19.u: You need attitudes and perceptions side by side.
KM-19.g: Comparable profiles and the scales where they differ.

T: The journey map covers only the middle
People drop off before they start, or nothing happens after they leave
st: Choose the experience and lay out five stages: attract, enter, engage, exit, extend.
Fill in what happens at each stage today.
Judge each stage on what makes an experience hold: clear, fresh, absorbing, easy to reach, meaningful, and whether it changes something for the person.
KM-20.w: Putting all the detail into Engage and leaving the other four thin.
KM-20.wh: A five-stage view of an experience (attract, enter, engage, exit, extend) that looks before and after the main event.
KM-20.u: The whole arc matters, including how people arrive and what stays with them.
KM-20.g: A five-stage journey with its weak stages marked.

T: Research is done and people ask "so what?"
Findings sit in ten places
st: Collect the key findings and insights from all the work.
Build a table: finding, insight, design principle.
Arrange it as one diagram that shows how they connect.
Write a short description and walk the team through it.
KM-21.w: Design principles that do not trace back to any finding.
KM-21.wh: One page that links findings to insights to design principles, closing the research.
KM-21.u: At the end of analysis, before generating ideas.
KM-21.g: Design principles tied to the evidence behind them.

T: Brainstorms drift away from the research
You want ideas for every need, not only the obvious ones
st: Choose two sets of factors from the research (for example, user types and needs).
Set them as the rows and columns of a grid.
Fill each cell with one or more concepts.
Find the empty and crowded cells and push further.
KM-22.w: Two sets of factors that overlap, so that every cell says the same thing.
KM-22.wh: A grid that crosses two sets of research factors and asks for a concept in every cell.
KM-22.u: Insights are in hand and ideas must stay tied to them.
KM-22.g: A grounded, wide set of concepts.

T: People affected should shape the ideas
Roles and status in the room make people hold back
st: Prepare story cards, "what if" cards and a simple kit for making puppets and scenes.
People share everyday stories using the cards.
Small groups stage a scene with puppets, play it, film it, and talk it through.
KM-23.w: Treating the play as entertainment and losing what people showed you.
KM-23.wh: A co-design game in which mixed groups build and act out today's and tomorrow's scenes with puppets.
KM-23.u: Residents, staff and experts need to imagine together as equals.
KM-23.g: Acted scenarios and the ideas inside them.

T: Lots of single ideas, no whole solution
Good ideas compete when they could combine
st: Choose the categories a full solution must cover, drawn from user needs.
Sort the concepts into a chart, one column per category.
Build solutions by taking one concept from each column.
Compare the combinations and choose which to develop.
KM-24.w: Combining pieces that do not fit together, just to complete a row.
KM-24.wh: A chart that sorts concepts by category so whole solutions can be built by combining one from each.
KM-24.u: After idea generation, before choosing a concept.
KM-24.g: Several complete solution options and one chosen.

T: The concept has many parts that must work together
People cannot picture it from a description
st: Be clear on the solution and every part of it.
Create the characters and what they are trying to do.
Map their journey through the solution, scene by scene.
Sketch each scene with a caption, then rehearse the story aloud.
KM-25.w: Drawing only the happy path. Add the scene where it goes wrong.
KM-25.wh: A sequence of sketched scenes that shows how all the parts of a solution work for a person over time.
KM-25.u: A concept is chosen and must be made concrete cheaply.
KM-25.g: A storyboard others can react to.

T: Several solutions and limited resources
Good for users and workable for the provider are pulling apart
st: Write the criteria for user value and for provider value.
Plot them on a map: user value against provider value.
Discuss what to take forward, and what each score assumes.
KM-26.w: Reading team scores as evidence. They are assumptions until users and providers confirm them.
KM-26.wh: A map that scores each solution on value to users and value to the provider.
KM-26.g: A ranked set of solutions and the assumptions behind the ranking.

T: It worked in a workshop; will it work in real life?
A funder wants evidence before rollout
st: Choose what to pilot and write the pilot plan.
Choose a small real setting and get approval.
Run it, watch it, and revise from what you learn.
KM-27.w: Choosing the friendliest site and calling the result general.
KM-27.wh: A small-scale real launch of a solution, run to learn how it performs and how people experience it.

T: The strategy is agreed but nobody owns the doing
The organisation lacks a skill the solution needs
st: Review the strategy and the chosen solutions.
Describe how the context is changing.
Build a grid: solutions against the challenges of making them real.
For each cell, define the initiative, the owner and the timing.
KM-28.w: A plan with no owners and no named gaps.
KM-28.wh: A grid of solutions against implementation challenges, turned into initiatives with owners.
KM-28.u: After evidence, when it is time to make it real.
KM-28.g: An action plan with initiatives, owners and gaps.
